title: The Genitive
summary: The case of *of*: possession, origin, quantity, and the object of a negated verb. It is the commonest case in Lithuanian and the one an A1 learner meets in the most different jobs.

rules.heading: The Genitive Singular
rules.statement: The **genitive** answers *kieno?* (whose?) and *ko?* (of what?). Its singular endings are given below. Note that masculine **-is** and **-ys** fall together in **-io**, exactly as they fell together in the accusative (¶20), and that the genitive is the case in which a noun is cited second in every dictionary — it is what tells you which declension the word belongs to.

paradigms.caption: Nominative → genitive singular
paradigms.footnote: The feminines in -is decline apart: moteris → moters, naktis → nakties.

rules.heading: The Genitive of Possession
rules.statement: The possessor stands in the genitive and **precedes** the thing possessed, as in English "the brother's book" and never as in "the book of the brother". Lithuanian has no word answering to *of*: the ending does the whole work.

examples.note: proper names decline like any other noun

footnotes: Reversing the order reverses the sense: *mokytojo namas* is the teacher's house, *namo mokytojas* the house's teacher.

rules.heading: The Genitive of Origin
rules.statement: **Iš** (from, out of) governs the genitive, and with it a speaker says where they come from — one of the first things asked of a foreigner in Lithuania. The question is *Iš kur tu esi?*

rules.heading: The Genitive after a Negated Verb
rules.statement: The rule stated for recognition in ¶26 may now be given its reason. A negated verb asserts that **no part** of the thing was affected, and the genitive is the case of the part rather than of the whole; so the direct object of a negated transitive verb leaves the accusative and takes the genitive. This is not optional and admits no exception.

examples.target: Aš matau namą. → Aš nematau namo.
examples.gloss: I see a house. → I do not see a house.

examples.target: Ji turi knygą. → Ji neturi knygos.
examples.gloss: She has a book. → She has no book.

examples.target: Mes valgome duoną. → Mes nevalgome duonos.
examples.gloss: We eat bread. → We do not eat bread.

rules.heading: The Genitive of Quantity
rules.statement: A word of measure or quantity is followed by the **genitive** of the thing measured — the partitive genitive, so called because it names the whole out of which a part is taken. This is how prices are asked and shopping done, and it governs *kiek?* (how much, how many) as well.
footnotes: The genitive plural ends in -ų for every declension: namų, brolių, knygų, kačių. It is taken up in full with the plural.

rules.heading: Prepositions Governing the Genitive
rules.statement: Most Lithuanian prepositions govern one case and one only, and the commonest govern the **genitive**: *iš* (from), *nuo* (from, off), *iki* (until, as far as), *prie* (near, at), *ant* (on), *be* (without), *po* (after, of time). Learning a preposition means learning its case with it; a preposition with the wrong case is as wrong as a wrong preposition.

paradigms.caption: Prepositions with the genitive

rows.label: iš
cells: iš namo — out of the house

paradigms.footnote: Note that *ant*, on, takes the genitive where English feeling would expect a place-case; and that *po* with the instrumental means "under" instead, which is taken up with that case.

examples.gloss: The book is lying on the table.

rules.heading: Asking with the Genitive
rules.statement: The interrogative *kas* has its own genitive **ko** (of what), and for persons **kieno** (whose). A question is answered in the case the question word stands in — which is why knowing the case of a question word is knowing the shape of its answer.

examples.gloss: Whose book is this? — The brother's.
What do you not have? — Money.

vocabulary.notes: Irregular; learn the genitive with the word.

drills.stem: What is the genitive singular of **brolis**?
drills.explanation: Masculine -is makes -io. *brolį* is the accusative, which ends in a nosinė vowel (¶20).

The possessor takes the genitive and stands first, as in English "the teacher's house". *namas mokytojo* would be understood but reverses the natural order; *mokytojas* is the nominative and *mokytoją* the accusative.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš esu ____ Lietuvos.** (I am from Lithuania.)
drills.explanation: *iš* is "from, out of" and governs the genitive, which is why *Lietuva* appears as *Lietuvos*. *ant* and *be* also take the genitive but mean "on" and "without".

drills.stem: Which of these phrases are **correctly** formed?
drills.explanation: A word of quantity takes the genitive of what is measured, and so do *daug* and the preposition *be*. The last two should be *daug vandens* and *be pieno*.

drills.stem: *Mes valgome duoną.* Put into the negative.
drills.explanation: The prefix *ne-* is written onto the verb, and the object leaves the accusative for the genitive *duonos* — the negated verb asserts that no part of the bread was eaten, and the genitive is the case of the part (¶31).
*ant*, *iki* and *prie* all take the genitive. *į* takes the accusative and is the preposition of direction, taken up with the locative.

drills.stem: Complete: **Knyga guli ant ____.** (The book is lying on the table.)
drills.explanation: *ant* governs the genitive, so *stalas* becomes *stalo*. An English speaker expects a place-case here and must simply learn that *ant* is one of the genitive prepositions.

drills.stem: In which of these is the genitive used for a reason **other** than possession?
drills.explanation: Negation, quantity and origin respectively. Only *Rūtos katė* is possessive. The genitive is the busiest case in the language precisely because it does all four of these jobs.

drills.stem: **Aš matau didelį namą.** If the verb were negated, how many words would change form?
drills.explanation: Three: *matau* → *nematau*, and the object goes into the genitive with its adjective agreeing — *didelį namą* → *didelio namo*. Answering two means forgetting that the adjective follows its noun into the new case.

drills.stem: *Vanduo* (water) has the genitive *vandens*, not *vanduo* → *vanduos*. What does this show?
options: That a few common nouns decline irregularly and must be learned with their genitive.
That the genitive of -uo nouns is always -ens.
drills.explanation: The endings of ¶28 cover the great majority, but a handful of everyday words — *vanduo*, *skiemuo*, *sesuo* — stand outside them. This is why the dictionary cites the genitive: it is the form that cannot be guessed. Lithuanian has no neuter noun at all (¶10).

drills.title: Kavinėje
drills.passage: Petras yra iš Kauno. Jis dirba Vilniuje. Rytas. Petras eina į kavinę. Jis nori puodelio kavos ir duonos. Jis neturi pinigų — piniginė guli ant stalo namuose. Draugas Jonas duoda pinigų. Petras geria kavą be pieno.
drills.translation: Petras is from Kaunas. He works in Vilnius. It is morning. Petras goes to a café. He wants a cup of coffee and some bread. He has no money — his wallet is lying on the table at home. His friend Jonas gives him money. Petras drinks coffee without milk.

glossary.Kaunas: Kaunas, a Lithuanian city; gen. Kauno
glossary.Vilniuje: in Vilnius; the locative case, taken up later

questions.explanation: *Petras yra iš Kauno.* Vilnius is where he works, not where he is from — the passage keeps the two apart deliberately.

questions.stem: In the passage, which words stand in the genitive because of a **preposition**?
questions.explanation: *iš Kauno*, *ant stalo*, *be pieno*. *pinigų* is genitive for a different reason — the verb *neturi* is negated (¶31).

questions.stem: **Jis neturi pinigų.** If the verb were not negated, how many of the three words would change form?
questions.explanation: Two: *neturi* → *turi*, and *pinigų* → *pinigus*, the accusative plural. The pronoun *jis* is the subject and is untouched. Answering one is the usual slip: the case of the object changes with the verb, not merely the verb itself.
